chapter: The craft of the ad lib player
title: Playing Broadway shows: High Button Shoes opening night and Jamaica
summary: Stage mishaps, the changed role of the show bassist and subbing for George Duvivier in Jamaica.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Right. Well, maybe some of them had a bad night. Each night would be different. I was always asked about playing a show for a length of time. It changes with the performance. You know, things happen on stage, in the orchestra pit, and they're all things that keep you alert, you know, and you may be reading your book in the pit and you

hear a miscue on the stage, you're alerted to to that. And you have to adjust to the conductor and -- (Laughter.) -- on opening night I did 'High Button Shoes' with Phil Silvers, and this is my first big show. Number one, the light went out. So that held up the show. And we'd rehearsed --
You mean the light over your music stand.

Yeah, So the electrician's got to come from the top of the house all the way down through the theater into the pit and change the bulb. I can't touch it, you know. But we'd rehearsed the first part of it pretty thoroughly with Milton Rosenstock, and I turned the page too energetically and broke the book on the floor, and I had to play by ear -- (Laughter.) -- the first half of the show.
I thought you were an ad lib player.

Now the bass players play ad lib in the shows. Then it had to be -- precision, it had to be what was written. But I think from 'Jamaica,' I subbed for George Duvivier in 'Jamaica' in 1958, and he played ad lib all through the show. Then Aaron Bell came along and played ad lib all through his shows. So they just make notations and let you go for yourself, as long as
you're within the confines of what's going on. I like to play in shows.
